It will be dedicated to the nation on 21 November 2026 by Union Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan at NIHSAD. Avian influenza can cause near 100% mortality in infected poultry, triggering culling and trade restrictions with substantial financial losses for farmers. Since the disease was detected in India in 2006, more than 500 outbreaks have been reported. article.articleHeadline: Signs to recognize the four most common sexually transmitted diseases.
article.articleSummary: Vietnam highlights four common sexually transmitted infections: Chlamydia, Gonorrhea, Trichomoniasis, and Genital Herpes. Many STIs are asymptomatic yet transmissible, making safe sex and routine screening essential to prevent infertility and pregnancy complications. Chlamydia often has no early signs; when present, symptoms may appear 1–3 weeks after exposure and include painful urination, abdominal discomfort, discharge, and pain during sex. Gonorrhea signs typically emerge about 10 days after exposure and can include thick discharge and dysuria, with possible pelvic or rectal symptoms. Trichomoniasis, caused by Trichomonas vaginalis, may appear 5–28 days after contact; women commonly have vaginal discharge with odor, itching, and painful urination or sex. Genital herpes presents with red bumps, blisters, or ulcers and itching; the first outbreak is most severe, and transmission can occur without visible sores. Emphasizes prevention and treatment adherence.

article.articleHeadline: African swine fever outbreak detected in 12 communes and wards in Ninh Bình Province

The situation is described as complex due to weather and epidemiology; leadership, surveillance, and enforcement gaps in slaughter and transport controls, plus improper disposal of dead pigs and infected products, are highlighted. Provincial authorities mandate intensified, coordinated control measures, daily and weekly outbreak reporting, and strict regulation of pig movement within outbreak zones. Culling must follow veterinary law and the Ministry's guidance (Document 11145), based on professional diagnoses and conducted transparently. article.articleHeadline: Septic Shock Due to Pleural Empyema.
article.articleSummary: Septic shock due to left pleural empyema in a 35-year-old man with type 2 diabetes in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. He presented with fever, cough, and weight loss; hyperglycemia and septic shock were diagnosed, with pleural pus and infection spreading through the chest wall toward the left abdominal wall. CT showed bilateral inflammatory lesions with left lung volume loss, atelectasis and consolidation; the left pleural space contained many abscesses. Given high surgical risk in shock, a multidisciplinary team performed a minimally invasive drainage via a 1 cm incision at the left fifth intercostal space to drain pus and lavage the cavity, alongside antibiotics and metabolic control. After seven days, infection and respiration improved, the left lung re-expanded, and discharge followed. Prolonged hyperglycemia can impair immune function in diabetics, worsening infection outcomes.

article.articleHeadline: Review Links SFTS Virus Immune Evasion to Clinical Treatment Hurdles
article.articleSummary: SFTS virus (Dabie bandavirus) is a tick-borne pathogen causing severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome, first isolated in Henan, China (2009). China’s surveillance (2010–2023) reports 27,447 confirmed cases and an overall case fatality rate of 4.83%, falling from 12.68% in 2010 to 3.77% in 2023; hospital cohorts show 12–30% CFRs and ICU mortality around 50%. Designated a WHO priority pathogen since 2017, the virus reveals a widening gap between mechanistic understanding and clinical translation. Haemaphysalis longicornis is the main vector; other ticks (R. microplus, I. nipponensis, A. testudinarium) also transmit. Human cases occur in China, Japan, and South Korea; serological/animal evidence exists in Vietnam, Pakistan, Thailand, and Myanmar; H. longicornis has been detected in the United States, signaling spread risk. Human-to-human transmission occurs via blood/fluids; Zhejiang (2023) outbreak included seven of twelve infections from direct blood exposure. The virion is a three-segment RNA virus (L ~6,368 bp; M ~3,378 bp; S ~1,746 bp) with entry via clathrin-mediated endocytosis and receptors including DC-SIGN, CCR2, and LRP1. NSs and NP mediate potent innate and adaptive immune evasion, dampening IFN signaling and antigen presentation in monocytes and B cells.

article.articleHeadline: One Health: Severe H9N2 virus infection in a hospitalized patient without recognized poultry exposure
article.articleSummary: One new human infection with avian influenza A(H9N2) was reported from China (Hunan Province) to WHO during 6–12 November 2026. The patient is a pediatric resident with symptom onset 20 October 2026; exposure to household poultry was reported, and an environmental sample tested positive for influenza A(H9). All close contacts tested negative; the patient has recovered. Since 2015, 190 H9N2 infections have been reported in the Western Pacific Region, including 187 in China, two in Cambodia, and one in Viet Nam, with two deaths (both with underlying conditions). Most infections relate to poultry exposure and are mild; sustained human-to-human transmission is not evident, and community spread risk remains low. Genomic analyses identified A/Guangzhou/23127/2025 (H9N2), G57 genotype, HA lineage B, clade B4.7, closely related to local environmental strains. The findings stress severe disease without known exposure and the need for enhanced genomic surveillance.

Bordering Russia, Mongolia, China, and Kazakhstan are of particular concern. To prevent imports, the agency conducted 250 field inspections, 78 planned checks, and 26 investigative visits this year. Quarantine violations (Art. 10.6 of the Russian Code) incur fines: officials 15–30k rubles; citizens 3–5k; legal entities 50–150k. Transport of livestock without veterinary documents carries fines: citizens 3–5k; officials 30–40k; legal entities 300–500k. Monitoring includes hunting grounds and buffer zones around large poultry and pig farms; unauthorized cattle import is cited as a main outbreak driver.

article.articleHeadline: From an Eight-Bed Research Room in Ho Chi Minh City to a Milestone in Global Malaria Treatment.
article.articleSummary: OUCRU began in 1991 with eight-bed malaria unit at Ho Chi Minh City’s Infectious Diseases Hospital and has grown into an international network of 700+ staff across Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi, Nepal, and Indonesia, focusing on infectious diseases. Early artemisinin trials in severe malaria reduced mortality from ~40% to 10% by 2000 and informed Vietnam guidelines and WHO recommendations. The unit later studied typhoid fever, isolating multi-drug resistant Salmonella Typhi in An Minh, Kiên Giang, advancing antimicrobial resistance research. Other areas include tetanus, dengue, tuberculosis, meningitis, HIV, and emerging infections. OUCRU expanded to Nepal (2003), Hanoi (2006), and Indonesia (2008). It supported SARS, H1N1, and Covid-19 through RECOVERY; during a three-week hospital lockdown, it stored >10,000 samples and processed >2,000 daily, delivering genome sequences in 24–48 hours. D-Skepe for dengue and training local scientists are current priorities.

article.articleHeadline: Fungal Infections Identified in Non-ICU Pneumonia Patients Without Classic
article.articleSummary: Hanoi, Vietnam—National Lung Hospital conducted a retrospective cohort of 188 adults with community-acquired pneumonia admitted to general wards (Dec 2024–Jul 2025). Invasive pulmonary fungal infection developed in 12.8% of patients lacking classic immunosuppression. Clinically diagnosed fungal disease occurred in 24 patients (23 pulmonary aspergillosis, 1 mucormycosis). In-hospital mortality was 33.3% among those with invasive fungal infection vs 2.4% without (P<0.001). Multivariable analysis identified three independent risk factors: respiratory viral PCR positivity at admission (adjusted OR 3.15; 95% CI 1.26–8.18), diabetes mellitus (adjusted OR 4.10; 95% CI 1.45–11.55), and peribronchial infiltration on chest CT (adjusted OR 4.70; 95% CI 1.87–12.48). Diagnoses followed adapted 2019 EORTC/MSGERC criteria. Authors urge heightened vigilance and early fungal diagnostic evaluation for non-ICU CAP patients, especially diabetics or those with admission respiratory viral PCR positivity, given substantial mortality differences.

article.articleHeadline: Deputy Health Minister: Needs Many Innovations in Larval Control to Tackle Dengue.
article.articleSummary: As of 18 November 2026 in Jakarta, Deputy Health Minister Dante Saksono Harbuwono urged that dengue control in Indonesia requires multiple innovations in larval (Aedes aegypti) control, not reliance on community participation alone. article.articleHeadline: SIGAP-TB Arrives at Bhayangkara Hospital Semarang, TB Patients Monitored Until They Complete Treatment.

The appeal targets Central Java, including Banyumas and Cilacap, urging persistent vaccination and stakeholder engagement.

article.articleHeadline: BPOM-Bio Farma Develop AI for Testing Polio Vaccine.
article.articleSummary: Bandung, Indonesia – BPOM and Bio Farma are accelerating the use of artificial intelligence to test the safety of the poliovirus vaccine, focusing on neurovirulence testing to ensure no harmful effects on the nervous system. Currently, testing relies on animal models and manual histopathology readings of neural tissue, with hundreds to thousands of samples demanding high expert attention, lengthy processes, and fatigue risk. The AI system will read scanned tissue images using algorithms trained on standard criteria and prior results, aiming to speed and harmonize assessments. If successful, testing could be shortened by about 50%. Key steps include compiling standardized image datasets from Bio Farma and BPOM and integrating workflows in the Green Laboratory, with regulatory oversight to safeguard safety, quality, and efficacy—and potential new rules. The effort aligns with FDA/EMA standards, with deployment anticipated within one year.

Experts emphasize overcoming stigma, along with early case finding, active case finding, patient follow-up, and contact investigations. article.articleHeadline: World Health Organization: 2,000 cases of monkeypox per month worldwide, and new treatment guidelines.
article.articleSummary: WHO reports monkeypox transmission worldwide, averaging about 2,000 confirmed cases per month (Jan 2022–Aug 2026). At a virtual emergency seminar on clinical care, Dr. Rosamond Lewis outlined updated WHO guidelines grounded in new evidence. Transmission occurs via close contact, household exposure, sexual contact, and mother-to-child spread; pregnancy carries risk of miscarriage, with up to 50% reported. HIV infection and other sexually transmitted infections heighten susceptibility and risk of severe disease. Africa has seen Madagascar’s large, prolonged outbreak; the DRC struggles with diagnostic capacity amid other health crises, with more than 600 suspected cases monthly. Outside Africa, Brazil reports transmission; Pakistan sees rising cases with infant fatalities in health facilities; Afghanistan reports initial cases; Taiwan notes community transmission. Global risk remains moderate, higher for those with multiple sexual partners and children in endemic areas. Updates cover antiviral use, supportive care, and practical implementation in health facilities, alongside vaccination and surveillance.

article.articleHeadline: Itaverava records 6 positive COVID-19 cases, points to a new epidemiological bulletin - Correio de Minas

The Municipal Health Secretariat emphasizes preventive measures under the motto 'Prevention is still the best choice!'. The bulletin notes ongoing case surveillance and reiterates basic recommendations from health authorities, with no mention of hospitalizations or outbreaks beyond the six active cases in Itaverava. The update reflects routine public health monitoring and case management for COVID-19 in the municipality.

article.articleHeadline: Feira de Santana's Micareta 2026: Ronaldo's government prepares a health plan, dengue control, security, and changes to how commerce operates.
article.articleSummary: Feira de Santana’s Micareta 2026 launches with an integrated health and disease-prevention operation. The festival opens on 18 November 2026 with Mayor José Ronaldo de Carvalho presenting the city key to Rei Momo Marlon Santana. Health planning includes two urgent care units totaling 30 beds: a main unit with 24 beds at the intersection of Avenida Presidente Dutra and Rua João Durval Carneiro, and a second unit with 6 beds beside the Santuário Santo Antônio in Capuchinhos. Most cases will be treated within the festival circuit; transfers, when needed, go to UPAs and six municipal polyclinics, with complex trauma cases referred to Hospital Geral Clériston Andrade (HGCA). A mass-casualty drill (IMV) for about 100 participants is scheduled for 18 November at Unifacs to test command, triage, and transport protocols. Dengue prevention will be intensified, focusing on Aedes aegypti control in the Maneca Ferreira circuit during the event.

article.articleHeadline: Study identifies bacteria in roasted coffee samples.
article.articleSummary: Brazilian coffee study detects bacteria in roasted samples from Campinas, São Paulo. Researchers at the University of Campinas (Unicamp) analyzed 78 roasted coffee samples from 26 products (20 ground coffees and 6 bean coffees) across three production lots, sold in supermarkets in Campinas. Bacteria from nine genera and 18 species were identified, dominated by Bacillus (57.14%) and Staphylococcus (23.21%), with Staphylococcus warneri, Bacillus licheniformis, and Bacillus subtilis among the most frequent species; coliforms were detected in three ground coffee samples. No Salmonella or Escherichia coli were found. In a storage experiment, Staphylococcus epidermidis and Klebsiella pneumoniae remained viable in vacuum-packed coffee at 25°C for up to 42 days. However, conventional preparation with hot water and paper filters prevented recovery of tested microorganisms in the brewed beverage. The study emphasizes hygienic-sanitary controls post-roast, during grinding, handling, and packaging. Journal of Food Science, September 2026.

article.articleHeadline: Aparecida de Goiânia issues an alert after a 33% increase in meningitis cases - Brazil Urgente
article.articleSummary: Aparecida de Goiânia, Brazil, issued an epidemiological alert after a 33% rise in confirmed meningitis cases. By 2026-11-18, the city had 20 confirmed meningitis cases in 2026, up from 15 in all of 2025. Pneumococcal meningitis (Streptococcus pneumoniae) was the most common form in both periods. Meningitis can progress rapidly, causing serious complications, sequelae, and death. Vaccination is the main prevention. The alert was sent to public and private health facilities, including hospitals, UPAs, CAIS, and UBSs, to reinforce surveillance, early case identification, and immediate prevention and control. People with suspected meningitis should seek care promptly, ideally at a Unidade Básica de Saúde; more severe cases should go to a UPA or CAIS.

article.articleHeadline: Use of antibiotics without a prescription: experts warn about antibiotic-resistant bacteria in Paraná.
article.articleSummary: Paraná, Brazil — Experts warn that taking antibiotics without a prescription or stopping treatment early fuels antibiotic resistance and the emergence of 'superbugs.' The alert comes ahead of World Antibiotic Awareness Week, coordinated by the UN and WHO. The Paraná State Health Secretariat (Sesa) and the Regional Medical Council (CRM-PR) say self-medication can delay diagnosis, cause serious adverse reactions, and mask symptoms, underscoring the need for professional evaluation before antibiotics. Incorrect use—such as wrong dosing, skipping doses, or using antibiotics for viral infections like influenza or colds—can allow susceptible bacteria to be eliminated while resistant strains thrive, potentially requiring more toxic drugs. Disbiosis and allergic reactions are additional risks. In Paraná, pharmacies are routinely inspected, and the National Prescription Control System (SNCR) tracks controlled medications to strengthen oversight and promote electronic prescribing.

article.articleHeadline: Brazil sets up a crisis room after contact with an isolated group in the Amazon.
article.articleSummary: Brazil set up a crisis room by FUNAI and the Indigenous Health Secretariat (SESAI) after the first contact in 50 years between the Awá, an isolated Indigenous group, and neighboring Guajajara communities in Terra Indígena Arariboia, Maranhão. The contact occurred at Tauari village, where 15 Awá individuals—men, women, and children armed with bows and arrows—were seen receiving food from Guajajara in a forested area; Guajajara recorded images on mobile phones. The crisis room aims to guide regional staff on procedures and to avoid forced contact, given the heightened epidemiological vulnerability of isolated communities, which lack the same immunological defenses and risk death from diseases like influenza. Brazil counts about 114 isolated or lightly contacted groups. Authorities suggest the approach may reflect pressure from illegal invasions, deforestation, fires, and illegal mining/logging. The government emphasizes non-forced contact and continues protection programs and Guardiões da Floresta.

article.articleHeadline: Anvisa Bans Mozzarella Batch After Finding Bacteria; See Brand and Lot Number - Rnews
article.articleSummary: Brazil's Anvisa banned sale, distribution, and consumption of Italy brand sliced mozzarella after a lab test found Listeria monocytogenes in batch 180926. The measure, announced November 12, targets only this batch from Agroindústria Santo Anjo Ltda, with a voluntary recall by the producer. Consumers should check the lot code and must not eat any product labeled 180926, even if within shelf life or refrigerated. Listeria monocytogenes can cause listeriosis, with symptoms such as fever, muscle aches, nausea and diarrhea; severe cases include headache, neck stiffness, confusion, and neurological complications. At-risk groups include pregnant women, newborns, older adults, and the immunocompromised. Bacteria can multiply at refrigeration temperatures, so chilling does not ensure safety. Preserve packaging and proof of purchase, contact the seller or manufacturer for recall details, and seek medical care if symptoms appear.

article.articleHeadline: Brucellosis becomes notifiable; understand the disease.
article.articleSummary: Brazil's Health Ministry added human brucellosis to the list of compulsory notifiable diseases as of 17 November 2026, published in the Diário Oficial. Health services must report cases to the SINAN system; reporting can occur weekly from suspicion, without waiting for laboratory confirmation. Notifiable data enable detection of unusual case increases, contact tracing, and assessment of control policies to interrupt transmission. Brucellosis is a bacterial infection caused by Brucella species found in cattle, pigs, sheep, and dogs. Transmission occurs via consumption of unpasteurized milk and dairy products or raw or undercooked meat; inhalation of contaminated particles; and contact with infected animals or materials. High-risk groups include veterinarians, breeders, and slaughterhouse workers. Symptoms include fever, weakness, fatigue, loss of appetite, and body and head pains. Treatment uses antibiotics under medical supervision; there is no effective human vaccine.

article.articleHeadline: Venezuela strengthens epidemiological surveillance at regional health meeting in Bogotá
article.articleSummary: Venezuela joins nine Amazon basin and Darien Gap countries in Bogotá for the Technical Workshop and II General Assembly of the Amazon-Darién Network for Emerging Zoonoses with Epidemic Potential (Rade 2026). Participants from Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Guyana, Panama, Peru, Suriname and Venezuela advance unified early warning protocols for timely detection and risk assessment of zoonotic diseases—those transmitted between animals and humans—in border areas. The initiative, promoted since 2022 by PAHO and WHO with Pandemic Fund support, operates on a One Health framework integrating human, animal, and environmental health. The cross-border collaboration aims to optimize prevention and control of outbreaks with epidemic potential across strategic ecosystems of South and Central America.

article.articleHeadline: Leptospirosis: Ronaldo's government warns of contamination risks during the rainy season in Feira de Santrana and records three confirmed cases in 2026.
article.articleSummary: As of November 18, 2026, leptospirosis alerts persist in Feira de Santana, Bahia, Brazil, as intensified rains raise floodwater exposure. The illness is caused by Leptospira bacteria, transmitted mainly through contact with water or mud contaminated with urine from infected animals, especially rats. From January to October 2026, the Epidemiological Vigilance registered 11 suspected cases among Feira de Santana residents, with 3 laboratory-confirmed, 5 ruled out, 2 inconclusive, and 1 under investigation. In 2025 there were 19 suspected notifications, with 3 confirmed, 14 discarded, and 2 inconclusive. Symptoms include fever, vomiting, malaise, chills, headache, and muscle pains (notably calves). Incubation ranges 1–30 days (often 5–14). Prevention focuses on avoiding floodwater exposure, protecting skin injuries, and wearing waterproof footwear; prompt medical care is urged for compatible symptoms after flood exposure, to reduce severity and potential fatal outcomes.

article.articleHeadline: DRC-Bunyakiri: Following clashes between FRN and the army, insecurity is hampering access to healthcare in an area affected by cholera and malaria.
article.articleSummary: Cholera outbreak and a malaria surge in the Bunyakiri health zone, South Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo, amid intensified fighting between FARDC (backed by militias) and FRN since November 6, have driven mass displacement and disrupted access to healthcare and essential medicines. MSF warns that deteriorating security and reduced treatment capacity raise the risk for communities already burdened by disease. On November 13, drone strikes near Bulambika close to populated areas and the Bunyakiri Referral General Hospital, which MSF supports, prompted relocation of hospital services to Maibano and the transfer of 76 inpatients. The hospital had logged an average of over 1,280 admissions per month recently, including 1,438 in October. MSF temporarily reduced local staffing, relocating teams to Bitale and Bukavu to limit exposure, while continuing to donate medicines and supplies to district health centers. MSF calls on all parties to respect international humanitarian law and protect civilians and health facilities to ensure safe access to care.

article.articleHeadline: Mosquitoes brought dangerous Chikungunya fever to Switzerland.
article.articleSummary: Four autochthonous chikungunya cases were confirmed in Switzerland, all residents of the Ticino canton, with no recent travel to endemic areas. The infection source remains unidentified. Patients experienced joint pain; illness was generally favorable. The World Health Organization notes Asian tiger mosquitoes (Aedes albopictus) are established in several Swiss cantons, including Ticino, capable of transmitting chikungunya. Following case confirmation, authorities conducted active case finding, mosquito surveillance, vector-control measures, and risk communication to healthcare workers and the public. No new cases were detected. The WHO warned ongoing transmission could occur if the virus enters mosquito habitats, but the current risk is low due to seasonal reduction in mosquito activity. Separately, it was reported yesterday that since the May 15 outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ebola has infected over 11,000 people and caused over 5,500 deaths.

article.articleHeadline: Kenyan Peacekeepers Secure Civilians and Support Ebola Response in Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC)
article.articleSummary: KENYA Defence Forces’ 5th Quick Reaction Force (KENQRF 5) takes over a Static Combat Deployment in Nia Nia, Ituri Province, DRC, under MONUSCO to protect civilians and support the Ebola response. Assuming duties from the Nepal Quick Reaction Force after a Relief-in-Place, the two-month-old deployment continues MONUSCO’s security presence amid threats from illegal armed groups and ongoing Ebola outbreak efforts. KENQRF 5 will focus on protecting civilians, supporting Ebola prevention awareness, and securing treatment centres and other vital infrastructure to ensure uninterrupted access to healthcare for communities, healthcare workers, and partners. Beyond security, the unit will promote community confidence-building and public health messaging, acknowledging that effective disease containment depends on safe facility access and cooperation between security personnel, healthcare providers, and affected populations. The deployment reinforces Kenya’s role in MONUSCO’s mission to protect civilians and facilitate humanitarian access in Ituri.

article.articleHeadline: Africa: Artificial intelligence in the fight against polio.
article.articleSummary: World Health Organization (WHO) uses artificial intelligence to enhance poliomyelitis surveillance in Africa. The WHO Regional Office for Africa, based in Brazzaville, integrates AI into surveillance systems to speed case detection and monitor vaccination campaigns. Weekly data from 47 African countries cover poliovirus circulation, laboratory results, vaccination coverage, and surveillance activities. AI-powered GIS tools let staff query databases in plain language and automatically generate maps, tables, and summaries showing poliovirus detections by country, district, or period. This enables identification of areas with weak surveillance or suboptimal vaccination and cross-links surveillance with vaccination data to better target field interventions. It also helps track supplementary vaccination operations, pinpoint delays and logistical challenges, and speed responses to transmission risks. AI supports, not replaces, epidemiologists and human data checks, and was unveiled on World GIS Day, November 18.

article.articleHeadline: River Connectivity Restructures Mpox Transmission Risk Across Rural
article.articleSummary: Mpox incidence forecasts in Maï-Ndombe province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, improve when models incorporate multimodal river-road connectivity, but provincial-scale fit declines. In a 2022–2025 study published in the International Journal of Health Geographics, researchers integrated environmental friction surfaces with inter-zone interaction and a metapopulation S-E-I-R framework to quantify how riverways and sparse roads shape Mpox spread. Using a Fuzzy Analytic Hierarchy Process to derive barrier weights, dense forest and water emerge as dominant friction barriers (0.31 each), followed by hydromorphic zones (0.15), slope (0.12), forest mosaics (0.091), and savanna (0.053). Travel speeds of 30–50 km/h on roads and 5–10 km/h on navigable waterways feed a least-cost path and an enhanced gravity model, with origin zones (<50,000) seeding transmission to destinations (>50,000). Baseline transmission rate 0.4695; Monte Carlo simulations quantified diagnostic/reporting uncertainties. Findings show epidemic trajectories are conditioned by asymmetric connectivity rather than uniform spread.

article.articleHeadline: Shandong Listeria Study Links Food and Clinical Isolates Using Genomic
article.articleSummary: Listeria monocytogenes in Shandong, China, shows broad genomic diversity with close ties between clinical infections and contaminated foods. In 2023–2024, 156 isolates from food and patients were sequenced, revealing two evolutionary lineages, four serogroups, 21 sequence types, and 17 clonal complexes. The study identified 15 antimicrobial resistance genes (5 intrinsic), six plasmid types, and 11 prophage types, highlighting an accessory genome capable of gene exchange. High-resolution SNP analysis linked four clinical isolates to food isolates within 50 SNPs, and one food isolate to a clinical isolate within 20 SNPs, underscoring dietary sources as infection links. CC87 emerges as a high-priority lineage for surveillance due to virulence markers; whole-genome sequencing underpins source tracking and risk assessment.

article.articleHeadline: Brucellosis Knowledge Deficits and Behavioral Gaps Found Along Southwestern
article.articleSummary: Brucellosis knowledge deficits and behavioral gaps were identified along Guizhou Province’s cattle value chain in a study of 771 stakeholders (142 farmers, 123 slaughterers, 109 vendors, 397 consumers) conducted Aug–Oct 2024. Awareness averaged 49.59%—far below the 90% national target; 57.1% had heard of brucellosis and 46.7% recognized its zoonotic transmission. Farmers showed the deepest gaps (31.7% recognizing susceptible animal species; 25.4% aware of zoonotic risks). Positive attitudes prevail—61.2% prioritize preventing human transmission; 68.6% willing to participate in education, with 89.4% of farmers and 93.6% of vendors open to training. Yet only about one-third consistently adopt safety measures; PPE use remains low, especially for masks and boots, despite high willingness (vendors 90.8% vs actual use). Attitude-practice correlation strongest (rs=0.299). Slaughterers and vendors had higher KAP than farmers/consumers, signaling need for node-specific interventions in this endemic setting.

article.articleHeadline: Surveillance Across China Identifies High PRRSV2 Prevalence and Extensive
article.articleSummary: PRRSV2 remains the dominant swine pathogen in China. A 2022–2025 nationwide survey across 30 provinces analyzed 23,962 clinical samples from pigs with abortion or respiratory signs; 7,977 were ORF6-positive by qRT-PCR, for an overall positive rate of 33.29% (95% CI 32.69–33.89). Four major lineages circulate (1, 3, 5, 8) with sublineages 1.8 (NADC30-like) and 1.5 (NADC34-like) prominent. ORF5 sequencing of 2,433 field samples yielded: sublineage 1.8 1,171 sequences (48.13%), sublineage 1.5 394 (16.19%), lineage 8 398 (16.36%), lineage 5 286 (11.76%), lineage 3 184 (7.56%). Historically, lineage 8 predominated before 2013; 1.8 emerged in 2013; 1.5 arose in 2017. Phylogenetic analysis used MEGA 11 (1,000 bootstrap) on ORF5. The study confirms persistent, widespread circulation of PRRSV2 in Chinese swine herds during 2022–2025.

article.articleHeadline: Gut Bacterium Parabacteroides distasonis Alleviates ETEC Diarrhea in Weaned
article.articleSummary: Parabacteroides distasonis HNAU0205 mitigates Escherichia coli enterotoxigenic (ETEC) diarrhea in weaned piglets from Ningxiang, Hunan, China. In a 24-piglet 2x2 factorial trial (control, ETEC challenge, P. distasonis alone, and P. distasonis plus ETEC), 21-day-old crossbred barrows received daily oral gavage of 1×10^9 CFU/mL P. distasonis (10 mL) for 14 days, with ETEC K88 challenge on day 15 and continued dosing until day 17; euthanasia with tissue sampling on day 18. Prophylaxis reduced ETEC-associated weight loss and significantly lowered diarrhea rates. ETEC density in ileal mucosa decreased; tight junctions were reinforced, circulating bacterial toxins and pro-inflammatory cytokines declined, and intestinal stem cell–driven epithelial renewal was stimulated, preserving growth. Fecal secretory IgA levels correlated with Parabacteroides distasonis abundance, supporting microbiome-based nutritional strategies to protect piglets during weaning and reduce antimicrobial use.

article.articleHeadline: Climate Models Project Shifting Echinococcosis Transmission Risk Across
article.articleSummary: Western China faces climate-driven shifts in echinococcosis risk. Ecological niche modeling of Echinococcus multilocularis (alveolar echinococcosis) and Echinococcus granulosus sensu lato (cystic echinococcosis) predicts nonuniform geographic reconfiguration under warming. Using 1981–2010 baseline climates, MaxEnt models trained on 1,247 unique human cases (1981–2016) from the National Echinococcosis Control Program across Gansu, Ningxia, Xizang, Qinghai, Xinjiang, and western Sichuan show six provincial-level regions with heterogeneous suitability changes: high-altitude plateaus gain suitability for both species, while arid and low-elevation margins contract. CE (E. granulosus s.l.) begins expanding outward from current endemic boundaries; AE (E. multilocularis) shifts into higher elevations. Model performance was excellent (mean training AUC >0.96; Boyce indices 0.886 for AE, 0.984 for CE) with 10-arc-minute grid cells and CHELSA 2.1 bioclimatic predictors; results emphasize distinct thermal and hydrological thresholds shaping each parasite's risk.

article.articleHeadline: The genetic test that discovered COVID-19 and that now saves lives by detecting almost all infections.
article.articleSummary: In December 2019, virologists in three Chinese cities analyzed samples from hospitalized patients with severe pneumonia who had visited the Huanan seafood market in Wuhan. For example, Dr. Charles Chiu treated a patient with meningitis and liver failure; metagenomics identified hepatitis E, allowing antiviral therapy and avoiding liver transplantation. Previously, sequencing took days to weeks, but modern machines deliver results in 1–2 hours with AI, accelerating care for immunocompromised patients such as transplant recipients, cancer patients, and those with autoimmune diseases. As of 2026-11-18.

article.articleHeadline: Platelet to Pleural Fluid ADA Ratio Identifies Tuberculous Pleural Effusion
article.articleSummary: Retrospective, single-center study in Xinxiang, China (The First Affiliated Hospital of Henan Medical University) analyzed 184 pleural effusion cases from 2020–2023 to assess the peripheral platelet-to-pleural fluid ADA ratio for diagnosing tuberculous pleural effusion. A public health framework—Integrated Prevention and Control of Four Diseases (enacted 2021) and a precision management model piloted in 2017 and expanded to 17 counties by 2021—employed opt-out testing and multi-tier governance to address co-infection. article.articleHeadline: Infant Meningitis Case Linked to Suspected Neurogenic Lower Urinary Tract
article.articleSummary: Two-month-old male infant with protracted meningitis caused by extended-spectrum beta-lactamase–producing Escherichia coli (ESBL-EC) at South China Hospital and Shenzhen University. The infection led to septic shock and subdural fluid collections. Despite meropenem, fever and abnormal subdural fluid persisted; intermittent dexamethasone and neurosurgical subdural drainage were performed. Serial neuroimaging revealed extensive brain injury with bilateral frontal cortical encephalomalacia and left temporal encephalomalacia, plus intracranial hemorrhages. At five months, urological evaluation showed neurogenic-type lower urinary tract dysfunction: reduced bladder compliance, detrusor overactivity, and elevated post-void residual; left vesicoureteral reflux grade III. Spinal MRI excluded gross cord lesions, though localization to supraspinal micturition centers remained uncertain. Management included clean intermittent catheterization and antibiotic prophylaxis; recurrent febrile UTIs occurred. Growth deceleration was noted between six and twelve months, with partial stabilization by fifteen months. The authors emphasize early multidisciplinary care and need for further research on antibiotic/corticosteroid regimens in severe pediatric CNS infections.

article.articleHeadline: Global Systematic Review Reveals High Toxoplasma gondii Diversity in Camels
article.articleSummary: Toxoplasma gondii shows high genetic diversity in Camelidae and Equidae worldwide, based on a systematic review of 20 studies (103 isolates) across five continents. Unlike human/ruminant populations where Type II dominates, these hosts harbor predominantly atypical and mixed genotypes, highlighting their value as sentinels of regional parasite diversity. Americas (17 isolates) lacked Type I/III, with 88.2% atypical; Africa (18 isolates) had no Type I and 83.3% atypical. Asia (54 isolates) displayed the greatest complexity, with 61.1% mixed infections; China I (ToxoDB #9) emerged as the dominant single lineage. Europe (14 isolates) was dominated by Type III (57.1%). Phylogenetic analysis using 11 multilocus markers grouped isolates into three core lineages (Type I–III). Environmental exposure to diverse oocysts appears to drive infection, underscoring camelids/equids as potential reservoirs of zoonotic, genetically complex T. gondii strains.

article.articleHeadline: Geminivirus Betasatellite Subverts Plant Coat Protein Resistance to Enable
article.articleSummary: Field surveys in October 2024 in tomato greenhouses at Hangzhou, Zhejiang, China identified co-infections of tomato leaf curl New Delhi virus (ToLCNDV), tomato yellow leaf curl China virus (TYLCV-China), and TYLCV with the betasatellite TYLCCNB. The study shows βC1, a betasatellite effector, binds the ToLCNDV coat protein (CP) and directs its ubiquitin-proteasome–dependent degradation, disabling CP-mediated resistance and permitting systemic infection by the viral genome in foliar tissues. Coat protein–mediated resistance has long been used by expressing viral CP to block uncoating, replication, movement, and to trigger RNA silencing and defense signaling. The authors generated transgenic Nicotiana benthamiana expressing ToLCNDV CP; CP accumulation was confirmed by immunoblot. When challenged with TYLCV alone, coat protein–expressing plants developed substantially.

article.articleHeadline: US Loses Measles-Free Status After 26 Years As Outbreak Hits 5,412 Cases In 2026: Could This Be A Warning For India?
article.articleSummary: US measles outbreak 2026 reaches 5,412 confirmed cases through November 12, ending 26 years of elimination after PAHO confirmed continuous circulation for over 12 months on November 17, linked to the 2025 Texas outbreak. In India, vaccination improved to 98% first-dose and 95% second-dose in 2025, but ~4.53 lakh children missed first dose; 18,774 cases in 2025 and ~26,627 in the first half of 2026, with endemic transmission ongoing. article.articleHeadline: ICMR launches infectious disease surveillance network for early outbreak warnings
article.articleSummary: ICMR launches a syndromic surveillance initiative for infectious diseases in India to provide early outbreak warnings. The network links 70 Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs) and Infectious Disease Research & Diagnostic Laboratories (IRDLs) to collect real-time data for rapid analysis of outbreak size, spread, and speed. It replaces fragmented, disease-specific testing with India-specific priority pathogen lists for major syndromes—Acute Febrile Illness (including Acute Undifferentiated Fever, Fever with Rash, Fever with Lymphadenopathy), Acute Encephalitis Syndrome, Acute Respiratory Illness, and Acute Diarrhoeal Disease—to guide diagnostics, surveillance, and policy. Pathogens are graded from Priority 1A (common) to 3 (rare). High-priority factors include endemic or outbreak-prone areas, post-monsoon and flooding seasons, animal exposure history, and screening a subset of negative samples. The framework also supports indigenous industry partners in developing cost-effective countermeasures.

article.articleHeadline: Surveillance Identifies Antimalarial Resistance Mutations in Southwestern
article.articleSummary: Clinical surveillance of Plasmodium vivax in southwestern India identified widespread antimalarial resistance mutations across Pvmdr1, Pvcrt-o, Pvdhfr, and Pvdhps in 93 isolates from symptomatic adults collected July 2021–September 2024 at Kasturba Medical College (Manipal), Udupi District Hospital, and Mangaluru District Hospital. Pvmdr1 mutations: M908L in all samples; T958M and F1076L in ~86% and ~85%; Y976F in 2.15%. Pvcrt-o showed a K10 insertion in 26%. Folate-pathway mutations included Pvdhfr S58R (59.13%) and S117N (56.98%), with the S58R+S117N haplotype most common; Pvdhps A383G (26.88%) and A553G (13.97%). While not indicating complete chloroquine resistance, the Y976F mutation in two samples has been linked to reduced chloroquine susceptibility. Authors call for continued molecular surveillance and region-specific antimalarial strategies to address rising resistance in this region.

article.articleHeadline: First Case of Disseminated Mycobacterium sherrisii Reported in Indian HIV
article.articleSummary: First reported case of disseminated Mycobacterium sherrisii infection in India, in a 40-year-old man from Maharashtra with advanced HIV (CD4 65 cells/µL). After three months on antiretroviral therapy (ART) and empiric four-drug anti-tubercular therapy at Poona Hospital, he developed immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) with fever, abdominal distension, and watery diarrhea. Ascitic fluid and stool cultures yielded atypical mycobacteria; PCR ruled out Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, and MALDI-TOF confirmed Mycobacterium sherrisii. Drug susceptibility testing followed. Therapy was adjusted to a targeted regimen of clarithromycin, ethambutol, and rifabutin, with corticosteroids while continuing ART. The authors emphasize that disseminated M. sherrisii closely mimics tuberculosis, making rapid species-level identification and macrolide-based treatment crucial for outcomes in advanced HIV. This case represents India’s first reported disseminated M. sherrisii infection; rising non-tuberculous mycobacterial diagnoses are linked to molecular diagnostics.

article.articleHeadline: Farmers demand relief as lumpy skin disease ravages native Pulikulam calves
article.articleSummary: Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD) is ravaging Pulikulam cattle in Tamil Nadu's Madurai district, with farmers claiming at least 1,000 Pulikulam calves have died since August 2026. Officials say no official cow deaths linked to LSD and note a lack of breed-specific mortality data. The Tamil Nadu Federation of Pastoral Peoples Sangams (TFPPS) warns of a widening outbreak across the district, estimating a minimum economic loss of ₹1 crore (≈ ₹10,000 per calf). They demand ₹10,000 compensation per calf and early-August vaccination campaigns, plus strengthening of the 1962 Mobile Veterinary Service to reach grazing herds. They encourage integrating traditional herbal veterinary practices, including Punniyamoorthy’s betel-leaves-salt-pepper formulation, pending scientific evaluation. Government vaccination drives continue, but some farmers fear reduced milk production from vaccination; authorities urge uptake and direct outreach to pastoral communities.

article.articleHeadline: ICMR Flags Widespread Antibiotic Resistance Across India: From E. coli To Typhoid, Which Drugs Are Failing?
article.articleSummary: India's ICMR AMRSN Annual Report 2025, released 2026-11-18, analyzes Gram-negative bacteria (E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa) and Gram-positive Staphylococcus aureus/Enterococcus across 34 secondary-care hospitals. E. coli shows low susceptibility to third-generation cephalosporins: cefotaxime 18.4%, ceftazidime 24.7%; OPD isolates indicate community resistance. In K. pneumoniae, susceptibility to piperacillin-tazobactam 29.2%, third-gen cephalosporins 23–27%, carbapenems 35–40%, amikacin 44.5%, ceftazidime-avibactam 37.7%, with tigecycline at 79.3%. E. coli ceftriaxone susceptibility across hospital categories falls from 39.8% (Category I) to 11.5% (Category III); meropenem from 80.3% to 67.1%. A. baumannii shows 91.1% carbapenem resistance; OXA-23 dominant, often with NDM co-profiles. S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi A show very low ciprofloxacin susceptibility (2.0% and 0.4%). The report underscores urgent need for diagnostics, rational antibiotic use, and infection prevention to curb resistance in India.

article.articleSummary: 2,839 active TB cases in Bhiwandi, including 1,603 women, 1,236 men, and 230 children up to 14 years; women outnumber men by 367. Dr. Bushra Sayed, TB Department in-charge, directed intensified screening, regular treatment, and expanded Nikshay Mitra support to meet year-end targets and accelerate case finding, reintegrating those who paused testing or treatment. A review with Doctor For You stressed sustaining momentum, counseling reluctant individuals, and engaging corporators and affluent residents to bolster patient aid. Stigma and delayed diagnosis were highlighted as risks that can worsen outcomes, with residents urged to seek medical examination promptly as part of ongoing TB management in Bhiwandi on 2026-11-18.

article.articleHeadline: HIV in all 23 districts of Haryana by December 31 | UNI Varta.
article.articleSummary: Chandigarh, November 18, 2026 — Haryana aims to bring all 23 districts under the HIV/AIDS Safe District framework by December 31, 2026. The Health and Family Welfare Department directed accelerated HIV testing, treatment access, and regular patient monitoring to achieve uniform control statewide. Additional Chief Secretary Dr. Sumita Mishra announced the target at the Chandigarh workshop titled 'Secur ity Pledge' (सुरक्षा संकल्प कार्यशाला), noting that HIV testing coverage rose from 85.2% in July 2026 to 94.7% in October 2026. The initiative emphasizes expanded testing, ensured linkage to care, initiation of antiretroviral therapy, and ongoing surveillance across districts. The report does not provide district-level case or mortality figures. If realized, the plan would signify comprehensive HIV containment across Haryana, aligning preventive and treatment services with the Safe District objective.

article.articleHeadline: Mosquito menace stings Hyderabad
article.articleSummary: Hyderabad reports a rising mosquito menace across almost all localities, with swarms entering homes after sunset and intensifying at night despite authorities' claims of control. Residents cite sharp evening spikes in nuisance from Old City, Golconda, Nampally, Red Hills, Rajendranagar, Banjara Hills, Jubilee Hills, Film Nagar, Madhapur, Kukatpally, KPHB, Uppal, LB Nagar, Tolichowki (Samatha Colony), Mallepally, and Begumpet, plus along the Musi riverbank where open nalas breed. Daytime levels are tolerable, but evening-to-night swarms persist, forcing nets, repellents, and electric devices. Hospitals report fever, body aches, cough, and cold; suspected dengue and influenza-like illnesses add to the health burden. In Malkajgiri’s ICRISAT Enclave, over 50 families warned of dengue, malaria, and chikungunya fears. GHMC says fogging and anti-larval operations run daily; residents urge intensified fogging, drain cleaning, and garbage removal. A four-week sanitation drive since November 9 covers 30 GHMC circles.

article.articleHeadline: Govt sets national guidelines for sewage testing as early warning tool to detect disease outbreaks
article.articleSummary: India publishes National Guidelines on Wastewater Surveillance for Pathogens, developed by NCDC and APSI-India, released by Dr Rakesh Gupta. The guidelines standardize sample collection, testing, and interpretation with IDSP to use wastewater as a warning tool for pathogens and disease trends. They list priority targets: poliovirus, SARS-CoV-2, influenza, RSV, measles, hepatitis A and E, dengue, and cholera; plus antimicrobial resistance genes and unknown pathogens. Sampling can occur at sewage treatment plants, sewer networks, open drains, and hospital outlets; catchments of 100k–300k people in cities; avoid septic tanks, latrines, or open fields. Routine sampling: weekly or biweekly; results uploaded to IHIP within 48 hours; escalations if a serious pathogen is detected, levels rise over two consecutive cycles, or a novel variant is found. Use includes targeted diagnostics, vaccination drives, GIS mapping, and water-quality actions; AMR monitoring is exploratory. Limitations: cannot identify individuals or exact case counts; trends require multiple sampling points.

article.articleHeadline: New dengue test promises early detection
article.articleSummary: Lucknow-based CSIR-NBRI hosted the 73rd annual day lecture where Padma Shri Navin Khanna highlighted an indigenous dengue diagnostic kit developed with ICGEB that can detect dengue from the first day of fever, unlike conventional tests that confirm later. The technology, presented at the event, aims to shorten the window to treatment and help prevent severe complications. NBRI director Zabeer Ahmed noted ongoing interdisciplinary collaboration and industry partnerships. In the year, NBRI reported 185 research papers, two Indian patents, and four patent applications (including one international filing).

article.articleHeadline: Power Of Community Support Systems In Defeating Drug-Resistant TB
article.articleSummary: MDR-TB case in Delhi highlights community-driven support as essential for treatment adherence. Mahesh, a 55-year-old daily-wage worker in a central Delhi urban slum, was diagnosed with multidrug-resistant TB in early 2025 after X-ray, sputum, and ultrasound investigations at Jhandewalan Chest Clinic and Dr NC Joshi Memorial Hospital. Diagnosis led to treatment initiation in April 2025, but livelihood pressures caused a treatment interruption as he sought work out of town. In October 2025, HPPI frontline workers Shimpi and Geeta (a TB survivor) conducted door-to-door screening, provided counselling, built trust, and coordinated with public services to restart therapy. Mahesh resumed a seven-tablet daily regimen at the chest clinic, despite hot flushes, until a leg fracture required bedrest, posing another risk of interruption. The case underscores the need for integrated community, health system, and social protection support to sustain MDR-TB treatment, echoed during World AMR Awareness Week 2026 and the Union World Conference on Lung Health.

This effort reflects ongoing public health measures in the region to reduce transmission and morbidity from onchocerciasis through targeted interventions in high-risk districts.

article.articleHeadline: Ghanaian Hospital Study Finds Intestinal Parasite Infection in Eleven
article.articleSummary: Intestinal parasitic infections were detected in 11.1% (394/3,542) of pregnant women attending antenatal care at Tamale Teaching Hospital in Northern Ghana (2021–2023), with 88.9% negative (3,148). Direct saline wet mount microscopy analyzed archived records; data capture was 97.82% from 3,621 identified. The Northern Ghana setting is described as underdeveloped with limited water, sanitation, and hygiene. Parasites include Entamoeba histolytica/dispar, Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris, hookworms, and Strongyloides. Maternal intestinal infections are linked to malnutrition, anemia, premature birth, impaired fetal development, and reduced birth weight; in severe cases, maternal-fetal death is possible. Globally about 24% are infected, with higher burdens in sub-Saharan Africa. Prior Ghanaian data show Central Region 19.3% and Ashanti 36.7%. Tamale serves five northern regions and neighboring countries, underscoring the regional relevance of antenatal parasitic surveillance.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue cases surge in Eastern Visayas, Bohol
article.articleSummary: Dengue infections surged in Eastern Visayas and Bohol, Philippines, with the DOH reporting 6,710 cases in Eastern Visayas from Jan. 1 to Nov. 7, including 12 deaths, a 110% rise from 3,194 in the same period last year. Leyte Province accounted for the largest share (2,142 cases, 32% of the regional total), followed by Northern Samar (1,403), Samar (861), and Tacloban City (790). Regional fatalities include Leyte (5), Northern Samar (3), Eastern Samar (2), and Samar (2). In Bohol, dengue rose by 133% to 5,319 cases and 25 deaths over Jan. 1–Nov. 7, up from 2,282 last year. Tagbilaran City led with 10.7% of provincial cases, and four dengue-related deaths were recorded there; other municipalities included Talibon, Inabanga, Ubay, and Getafe. Dengue is transmitted by Aedes aegypti; symptoms include high fever, severe headache, joint pains, nausea, vomiting, and rashes. Authorities urge community cleanup, elimination of standing water, and protective measures.

article.articleHeadline: Dabie Bandavirus Fatality Linked to Genotype B in Coastal East Asia
article.articleSummary: Dabie bandavirus–driven severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) shows inland-high-incidence versus coastal-high-fatality in East Asia. In 2010–2023 China recorded 27,457 cases and 1,326 deaths across 27 provinces, with 99.05% of infections and 99.62% of fatalities in seven core inland provinces. Inland provinces (Henan, Hubei, Anhui) had 7.31/100,000 incidence and 2.61% case fatality, while coastal Zhejiang, Jiangsu, Shandong, and Liaoning had 3.84/100,000 and 8.04% CFR (coastal infection RR 0.52; coastal CFR ~3.08× inland). One-month lag analyses link higher infection risk to warmer temperatures: inland Xinyang peaks at 20.6°C (RR 4.85), coastal Zhoushan at 22.6°C (RR 3.07); sunshine >200 hours/mo elevates coastal risk. Genomic analysis of 1,820 genomes reveals five genotypes (A–E); inland provinces harbor genotypes A/C/D, while coastal Zhejiang aligns with genotype B clades shared with Japan, Korea, and Thailand. Zhejiang shows marked micro-evolutionary compartmentalization between Xiangshan and Ningbo.

article.articleHeadline: Passengers on 2 Thai Airways flights urged to watch for measles symptoms
article.articleSummary: Measles exposure linked to two Thai Airways flights (TG340 Dhaka–Bangkok, seat 46D; TG475 Bangkok–Sydney, seat 36D). An infectious traveler who flew from Bangladesh to Bangkok before continuing to Sydney developed fever, cough, runny nose and sore throat on Nov 2, with a rash appearing Nov 8; laboratory-confirmed measles. The Sydney leg arrived Nov 7 at 21:10; the traveler sought care at Canterbury Hospital in Campsie on Nov 8. New South Wales health authorities issued a public health alert; information was shared with Thailand under IHR. Thailand's Department of Disease Control urged all passengers and crew on TG340/TG475, especially those near 46D and 36D, to monitor for 21 days after exposure (through Nov 28). Symptoms include fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes, and rash. If symptoms develop, avoid close contact, wear a mask, and report travel history. Bangladesh faces a major measles outbreak (>50,000 cases, ≥350 deaths).

article.articleHeadline: FAO promotes the One Health concept to prevent zoonotic diseases transmitted between animals and humans.
article.articleSummary: FAO promotes One Health to curb zoonotic diseases transmitted between animals and humans, highlighting that environmental degradation, climate change, and an El Niño-driven peak in late 2026 will worsen droughts, floods, water contamination from poultry farms, and cross-species pathogen spread. Three Asia-Pacific policy recommendations: (1) integrate wildlife and environmental context with human–animal disease surveillance to identify risks and justify biosecurity and ecosystem restoration; (2) invest in capacity building—experts, laboratories, veterinarians—to assess risk, monitor unusual diseases in wildlife and domestic animals, and communicate across sectors; (3) develop national plans with source-prevention measures, clear responsibilities, and sustained funding for wildlife and environment agencies to evaluate links among wildlife, livestock, and human disease risk. Thailand: FAO-supported avian influenza surveillance and cross-border control centers. Cambodia: wildlife health surveillance linked to human infection signals; H5N1 detected in poultry in March 2026 indicated human infection risk. Indonesia: training for wildlife/environment professionals; Sulawesi project unites government, researchers, and communities to mitigate zoonotic risk and conserve biodiversity.

article.articleHeadline: Zambia breaks ground on the first cholera vaccine plant.
article.articleSummary: As of 18 November 2026, Zambia began construction in Lusaka on its first cholera vaccine manufacturing plant, to be run by ZAMVAX Limited. The facility will have an annual capacity of up to 20 million doses and will start with fill-finish, finishing, packaging, and quality control of oral cholera vaccines from imported raw materials. The project is a public-private partnership between the state-owned Industrial Development Corporation (IDC) with 60% equity and China's Jijia International Medical Technology with 40%, featuring technology transfer, job creation, and strengthened national pharmaceutical capacity. It enables Zambia to shift from importer to regional vaccine producer. The move follows recurring cholera outbreaks, including the 2023–2024 epidemic that WHO counted at over 23,000 cases and more than 700 deaths, underscoring the need for greater vaccine availability.

article.articleHeadline: The Communicable Diseases Committee designates 'Polio' as a dangerous communicable disease; tightens controls on 'Rabies'.
article.articleSummary: On 18 November 2026, Thailand designates polio as a dangerous communicable disease under the 2018 Act due to import risk of vaccine-derived poliovirus from Laos and Myanmar, requiring laboratory confirmation for diagnosis. Rabies deaths reached 13 in 2026; authorities mandate integrated bite surveillance and rapid first-dose vaccination, with intensified animal vaccination and stray-animal control by the Department of Livestock, Local Administration, and allied agencies; public communication by the National Parks, Wildlife and Plant Department and Public Relations. The committee also approves two additional international border control points to facilitate trade, investment, transport, and tourism, with updates to the border-control working group. Influenza A/H1N1 accounted for 613,292 cases and 134 deaths in 2026, highest in ages 5–9 and 60+ with chronic disease. Other diseases: 32,007 cases and 7 deaths; 512 cases and 3 deaths (predominantly male with HIV co-infection); dengue in the south, 34,875 cases and 47 deaths; vector control urged and prompt hospital testing for suspected dengue.
